description: I'm a Software & AI Engineer, Full-Stack Developer, and Product Technologist passionate about astronomy, space exploration, and innovation. I created MARS LANDING, a 3D planetary exploration and survival game combining engineering, science, and interactive gameplay. My skills include AI integration, software development, and UI/UX design. I'm seeking teammates with expertise in aerospace engineering, astronomy, 3D game development, planetary science, and creative problem-solving.
summary:
MARS LANDING is an interactive 3D space exploration and survival game designed to introduce players to the challenges of planetary missions through immersive gameplay.

The project features five procedurally generated worlds where players pilot spacecraft, operate rovers, explore planetary surfaces, survey mineral deposits, repair communication towers, and manage critical survival resources such as oxygen, energy, and equipment integrity.

MARS LANDING addresses the challenge of making space mission planning, engineering, and exploration more accessible and engaging. By incorporating mission objectives, resource management, environmental hazards, and strategic decision-making, the game encourages players to think like engineers and space explorers.

The project demonstrates how interactive technology and gamification can inspire curiosity about astronomy, planetary science, and aerospace engineering. Its importance lies in making complex space exploration concepts approachable, particularly for younger generations, while encouraging problem-solving, creativity, and interest in future STEM careers.
details:
Mars Landing is a browser-based 3D space-expedition game.

You start by flying a lander through modelled atmospheric entry — a timed descent with hull shake, plasma streaks and terrain hazards — and touch down on a landing pad. From there you move between three play modes: on foot as an astronaut in first or third person, in the spaceship, and in a surface rover. On foot you scan mineral deposits and vents, repair comm towers, harvest ration pods, board the ship, and manage life support (oxygen, battery, jetpack, temperature). The ship allows interplanetary travel through a galaxy map; the rover carries an autocannon. Hostile fauna and ground-based anti-air batteries return fire, so combat, exploration and survival run together. Every discovery writes into the Xenocodex, pays credits, and those credits buy rifle marks, drive upgrades and consumables in the armory. Five difficulty tiers change incoming damage, enemy fire rate and life-support drain; at Hardcore and Impossible, death leaves your body behind as a spectral "ghost" you must return to a life-support station to reclaim. Scores and callsigns post to a global leaderboard, and a shared pilot chat runs inside the HUD.

Technically the game runs a fixed simulation loop over a procedural terrain height field: terrain, rocks, dust, sky and flora are generated deterministically from a seeded noise function, so every world is consistent between sessions without storing it. Movement resolves against terrain height, slab colliders, hull footprints and cave geometry, with gait animation driven by hip, knee and ankle rotation. All five worlds are modelled on real NASA fact-sheet values — surface gravity from 1.62 to 8.87 m/s², mean surface temperature, atmosphere, orbital period, axial tilt — so jumping, falling, life-support drain and sky palettes follow the actual body rather than an invented one.

**Benefits**

It runs entirely in a browser with no install, and scales its quality tier so the same build works on a laptop and a phone. Because the world is procedural and driven by data files, a new world is a data entry rather than a new level to hand-build. It doubles as science outreach: the Xenocodex, galaxy map and briefing screens surface real planetary figures (mass, diameter, orbit, day length, gravity, temperature) in the context of play, so players absorb accurate values while exploring.

**Intended impact**

The goal is to make planetary science feel physical. Rather than reading that Venus has 8.87 m/s² gravity and 464 °C surface temperature, you jump on it, watch your suit drain, and feel the difference from the Moon. It is aimed at players who want a system-rich survival game and at classrooms or science clubs that want an engaging entry point into comparative planetology.

**Tools, languages and software**

React 19 and JavaScript on the TanStack Start framework with Vite, hosted on Cloudflare Workers; Three.js for the WebGL renderer, procedural geometry, shaders and sky/materials; Tailwind CSS for the interface; Base44 as the backend platform for authentication, the entity database (leaderboard entries, chat messages) and file storage. Audio is synthesised at runtime through the Web Audio API. Assets are generated in code — textures, meshes, nebulae and ring systems are shader- and geometry-based — so there are no external art dependencies.

**How it's creative**

Three things. First, the environment is generated and physically grounded at once: a deterministic noise terrain, seen through a haze density derived from the player's chosen render radius, under skies matched to each body's real atmosphere. Second, the worlds are real: Titan's orange haze, Europa's ice shell fractured with ochre lines, Venus's unbroken sulfuric overcast, Jupiter and ringed Saturn placed correctly as neighbours, with an Earth in the lunar sky. Third, the fiction sits on top of the fact — hostile fauna, ruins and the Colossus are invented, but their homeworlds are not, and the codex clearly separates the two.

**Factors considered**

Cross-device performance (quality tiers, pixel-ratio caps, reduced particle and rock counts, context-loss recovery on mobile); accessibility and legibility of a dense HUD at both desktop and phone widths, including touch controls; fairness and tension in the difficulty curve, including the ghost-death rule so a wipe costs progress rather than ending the run; whether every number shown could be defended, which is why the planetary values were rebuilt from NASA data; clarity of the boundary between fact and fiction in the codex and records; and etiquette in shared spaces — the leaderboard and chat are player-generated and were treated as such, separate from the documented data.
